claim: Lakatos appraises a series of theories, not one theory: a hard core held fixed by methodological decision, a protective belt of auxiliary hypotheses that absorbs refutations, and a positive heuristic that plans the next models.
agent_test: Log core (task commitments) separately from patches; count patches per core in a run.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: A programme is progressive only if each revision has excess content over its predecessor AND some of that excess is later confirmed; revisions that only accommodate known facts are degenerating (ad hoc1 = no excess content, ad hoc2 = excess but none corroborated).
agent_test: Tag each S5 patch: does it predict an unseen case? Fire the impasse detector when K consecutive patches predict nothing beyond the failing example.

claim: Lakatos gives no number of failed steps or years after which to drop a programme; tolerance is open-ended (Prout 1815 to about 1911, Halley 72 years, Copernicus parallax 1838), so the criterion cannot serve as a stopping rule without added thresholds.
agent_test: Choose the stop threshold empirically (patch-count caps 1, 2, 3) at equal tokens; do not derive it from Lakatos.

claim: Lakatosian verdicts are retrospective and have reversed (Urbach IQ programme judged degenerating, Flynn effect 1987 reversed it; Mercury anomaly tolerated for decades). Hacking reads the rule as advice for historians, not for working scientists. Appraisal is not advice.
agent_test: Do not let a degenerating flag kill an attempt line permanently; keep best-so-far (G6) and allow one reopening at a budget fraction.

claim: Novelty is comparative and contested: a prediction counts only if rivals and conventional wisdom did not predict it (Lakatos), and Zahar lets known facts count if the core was not built to explain them. Judging novelty needs a reference set, and a model's own novelty claim is not valid.
agent_test: Operationalise novelty as: the patch predicts correctly on held-out inputs not used to build it, judged by code.

claim: Without an external signal, LLM self-patching does not help and often hurts. Huang et al. (ICLR 2024): GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 (3 calls) -> 41.8 (5 calls); GSM8K 75.9 -> 75.1 -> 74.7; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0; GPT-4 HotpotQA 49 -> 49 -> 43. Re-checked against the PDF.
agent_test: Run S5 with and without the located failing output at equal tokens; expect the no-output arm to be flat or worse.

claim: The apparent success of oracle-stopped self-correction comes from the stopping signal. Corrected figures from Table 2: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 84.3 (evidence line b14 said 95.5, wrong), CSQA 75.8 -> 89.7, HotpotQA 26.0 -> 29.0; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 97.5, CSQA 82.0 -> 85.5, HotpotQA 49 -> 59.
agent_test: Measure the gain of S5 when a held-out check decides whether to continue, versus a model-judged stop.

claim: Kamoi et al. survey: no major work shows successful self-correction from self-prompted feedback under fair settings; it works with reliable external feedback (tools, code execution) and after large-scale fine-tuning (SCoRe: +15.6 points MATH on Gemini 1.0 Pro, +9.1 HumanEval on 1.5 Flash). The bottleneck is generating feedback, not applying it. 2025 update: o1-preview and o1-mini also lose accuracy under intrinsic self-correction (Zhang et al.), so the result is not limited to older models.
agent_test: Compare S5 driven by code-located failures versus model-written critique, equal tokens.

claim: Self-repair of code is not clearly better than drawing more independent samples at equal cost (pass@t); feedback quality is the bottleneck. GPT-4 repair success with its own feedback 33.30% vs human feedback 52.60% (competition 3.67% vs 14.67%; 16 participants, 40 programs). Re-checked.
agent_test: Report pass@t for S5 versus the same budget spent on fresh samples.

claim: Extra debate or revision rounds do not beat plain sampling at equal calls: GSM8K GPT-3.5 self-consistency 82.5 (3), 85.3 (6), 88.2 (9) vs debate 83.2 (6), 83.0 (9). Re-checked.
agent_test: Already in schema (G9); keep as control.

claim: Self-verification by the same model is unreliable and degrades with repeated backprompts; a sound external verifier gives large gains (Stechly et al.). Models also show a self-correction blind spot: 64.5% average across 14 open models, cut 89.3% by appending 'Wait'. Re-checked for Tsui.
agent_test: Test a 'Wait'-style trigger inside S5 versus the plain revise prompt.

claim: Reflexion-style loops help when the test signal is reliable and hurt when it is not: HumanEval Python 0.80 -> 0.91 with test false-positive rate 0.01, but MBPP Python 0.80 -> 0.77 with false-positive rate 0.16. Re-checked.
agent_test: Gate S5 on the measured false-positive rate of the available check; skip revision when the check is weak.

claim: Repair loops show diminishing returns: AI Scientist v1 code edits fall 529 -> 118 -> 83 -> 66 -> 21 characters per iteration; shrinking edit size is a cheap degenerating proxy. Re-checked.
agent_test: Log patch size per round and fire S6 when it shrinks below a fraction of the first patch; test against a plain round cap.

claim: Later reasoning rounds add little: in o1-like models the first solution holds most correct answers; shortening cut tokens 48.6% on MATH500 at equal accuracy (QwQ-32B-Preview). Re-checked.
agent_test: Cap reasoning length and compare accuracy at equal tokens.

claim: The opposite failure also exists: abandoning a line too early. Wrong answers use 225% more tokens on average and more thought switches; a switch penalty lifts QwQ AIME2024 38.3 -> 44.1 and R1 73.8 -> 74.8, while a prompt to stay on one thought did not (R1 72.4). Re-checked.
agent_test: Test an S6 abandonment rule against a stay-longer rule; the stop threshold has two-sided risk.

claim: Patching a hypothesis bank from misfit examples works in labelled settings: HypoGeniC gains over few-shot of +31.7, +13.9, +3.3, +24.9 points; the update stage adds 0.7 to 8.1 points. Replacement is judged on known data, not novel facts.
agent_test: Keep 1 to 4 candidate rules, replace the worst on misfit examples, and check on held-out inputs (G3).

claim: A two-layer structure (abstract hypothesis as core, code as testable belt) beat direct prompting on ARC (100 tasks, GPT-4): 17% direct, 23% program only, 30% with generated hypotheses (LLM filter), 33% human-selected.
agent_test: Compare a rule-then-code scaffold against direct and program-only at equal tokens.

claim: Hard caps on debugging depth are used in agentic science systems (AI Scientist-v2: depth 3); its one accepted workshop paper (score 6.33, 3 of 43 submissions) was a negative result; independent evaluation of v1 found 42% of experiments failed and 57% of manuscripts had hallucinated numbers.
agent_test: The patch-depth cap is a design default; test caps of 1, 2, 3 on our tasks.

claim: Popper-style sequential falsification of single hypotheses has been automated (POPPER: Type-I error control, 10x less time than humans on biology hypotheses), but it tests single hypotheses, not sequences of patched theories.
agent_test: Not testable as a Lakatos claim; only borrow error control for G3.

claim: No study found directly measures an LLM against Lakatos's progressive vs degenerating test or core protection; the LLM evidence is indirect (self-correction, repair, hypothesis search). This is a coverage gap from rate-limited search tools, not proof of absence. Gap search 2026-11-03: one further search and the Denario paper (Lakatos only as philosophy) found no trace-labelling study; still unproven absence.
agent_test: Build the first test: log core and patches in transcripts, label progressive or degenerating post hoc by held-out prediction.

claim: A third category 'stagnant' (no progress for benign outside reasons) is proposed for physics (Branahl 2024/2026). It matters for an agent whose check is unavailable, where 'degenerating' would be the wrong label.
agent_test: In S0 mark problems with no available check; do not trigger a degenerating stop there, only accept the best attempt (G6).

claim: Critics hold Lakatos's rule unusable or empty: Feyerabend (any development can claim intermittent progress; waiting objection), Kuhn, Musgrave; Lakatos never showed scientists switched when the criterion fired; Laudan's problem-solving count is an alternative.
agent_test: Prefer concrete code-run progress signals to philosophical criteria.

claim: Meehl (1990) says shield the core only if the theory has a track record and high verisimilitude; this was seen only in a secondary snippet. Gap search: the primary PDF returned HTTP 403, still unread.
agent_test: Not testable until the primary text is read.

claim: A check with a false positive rate caps the value of retrying; the best number of attempts is finite and small once false passes cost something. At cost-benefit ratio 4 the optimal K is about 5 (HumanEval+, four models); weak models have more false passes and the rate rises with K. No study gives a single break-even false-positive rate for revision loops.
agent_test: In S0 estimate the check's false positive rate on a few items; set the patch cap from it and stop when a false pass costs more than a true pass gains.

claim: With a real external check, iterative repair gains come in the first 2-3 rounds: Self-Debug successes mostly end within 3 turns, CRITIC says 2-3 rounds give most of the benefit, S* plateaus after 2-3 rounds (QwQ-32B 72.6 to 74.2 at 2 rounds). Without a reliable check there is no such curve. These are code and math tasks; no study compares caps of 1, 2 and 3 at equal tokens, or exact-answer vs open problems.
agent_test: Default cap of 2-3 failed patches at S6 when a real check exists; test 1, 2, 3 on our benchmark.

claim: A model-generated test of a patch is not a reliable stand-in for a held-out prediction: in S*, debugging against model-generated tests gave no gain over public tests only, because wrong generated outputs add noise. The operational Lakatos excess-content test (predict an unseen case, then verify it) remains untested with an external verifier.
agent_test: Require the predicted held-out case to be checked by an external tool, not by the model.

claim: Revisions can destroy correct answers: 38% of correct answers were changed to incorrect by a naive revision model (Snell, MATH); o1-preview overturned 15.6% and o1-mini 34.0% of correct Yes/No answers under 'are you sure' prompts. A patch step needs a guard that keeps the prior best answer.
agent_test: Keep the best-so-far answer; accept a patch only if the check improves.

claim: Failed attempts left in context hurt: models rely on earlier incorrect attempts (39% average drop, 200,000+ conversations) and self-condition on their own errors, an effect the paper says is absent in recent thinking models. Pruning history to the last attempt only is mixed in code repair (helped one of three models). Whether a fixed core (S1 restatement) reduces drift under repeated patches is not directly tested; one study found re-appending the original question cut overturned answers by 5.3-10.9 points.
agent_test: A/B: patch with full history vs restart from the S1 task restatement plus only the last failure note.

claim: Both stopping errors are measured in traces: step repetition 15.7% and unaware of termination 12.4% vs premature termination 6.2% of annotated multi-agent failures (MAST, 1600+ traces). Extended thinking helps then hurts (GSM8K 82.2 to 87.3 at 1100 tokens, down to 70.3 at about 16,000); a forced floor helps AIME24 (50 to 57) but not MATH500. No study tests one adaptive rule against a fixed cap and a fixed floor.
agent_test: Gate floor and cap on difficulty from S0; log repeat rate as a degenerating signal.

claim: More visible reflection is not evidence of useful revision: R1-Zero self-reflection behaviours are not positively correlated with accuracy, and base models already show them. Cheap calibrated correctness signals exist in open models (hidden-state probe, ROC-AUC above 0.7, ECE below 0.1, 24% fewer tokens) but need model internals.
agent_test: Do not score progress by counting 'wait' or 'let me recheck'; score by external check change.
